extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying real analysis / basic topology (e.g., Math 104)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of textbook-style exercise prompts and hints for undergraduate real analysis and elementary topology (ordered fields, extended reals, complex field, Euclidean spaces, metric spaces). Each rubric is an exercise statement or subproblem specifying what to prove or construct, often with hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial eventual sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for a polynomial q(x) one of the following holds: (∃ B ∈ R) (∀ r ∈ R) (r > B ⇒ q(r) > 0) (i.e. q is 'eventually positive'), or (∃ B ∈ R) (∀ r ∈ R) (r > B ⇒ q(r) < 0) (i.e. q is 'eventually negative'), or q = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: look at the sign of the coefficient of the highest power of x in q(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions eventual sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce that if f is a rational function, then likewise either f is eventually positive, or f is eventually negative, or f = 0; i.e., (∃ B ∈ R) (∀ r ∈ R) (r > B ⇒ f(r) > 0), or (∃ B ∈ R) (∀ r ∈ R) (r > B ⇒ f(r) < 0), or r = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the behavior of numerator and denominator polynomials for large |x|; the text defines 'eventually positive/negative' analogously to the polynomial case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order on rational functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given rational functions f and f', write f < f' if f' − f is eventually positive. Show that this relation '<' makes the field of rational functions an ordered field F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the ordered-field axioms using the 'eventually positive' definition; verify compatibility of order with addition and multiplication (except trivial zero cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions field non-Archimedean
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that in F (the ordered field of rational functions) the polynomial x (regarded as x/1) is > n for all integers n, and hence F is not Archimedean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret x as the function f(r)=r and compare growth at infinity to constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small positive element 1/x in F
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce that the element 1/x ∈ F is positive but is less than all positive rational numbers (hence less than all positive real numbers); thus from the point of view of F the real numbers have 'gaps' between 0 and the positive reals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ordering and comparison with constants to show 1/x>0 but 1/x < 1/n for every positive integer n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation preserves least upper bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F be an ordered field. Suppose A ⊆ F has a least upper bound α ∈ F, and x ∈ F. Show that {a + x | a ∈ A} has least upper bound α + x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard property: translation preserves suprema; present direct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate arithmetic progression A = {n x | n ∈ Z}
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose x ∈ F and let A = {n x | n ∈ Z}. Show that {a + x | a ∈ A} = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic properties of integer multiples: adding x to every nx just shifts indices; demonstrate equality of sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexistence of least upper bound for integer multiples of nonzero x
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining the above, deduce that if x is a nonzero element of F then the set {n x | n ∈ Z} cannot have a least upper bound in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use translation-preserving-lub and invariance of A under translation to derive contradiction if a least upper bound existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean property via least upper bound property
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose x > 0 and F has the least upper bound property. From previous parts deduce that {n x | n ∈ Z} (and hence {n x | n ∈ J}) is not bounded above, and deduce the Archimedean property (Theorem 1.20(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that boundedness would produce a least upper bound contradicting (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction-like principle: definitions of (i)-(iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider statements P(x) about nonnegative real numbers and conditions: (i) P(0) true; (ii) For every x, if P(y) true for all y < x then P(x); (iii) For every x such that P(x) is true, there exists y > x such that for all z with x ≤ z ≤ y, P(z) true; (iv) For all x, P(x) true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These set up variants of an induction principle to be analyzed in parts (a)-(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: (i) and (ii) do not imply (iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that (i) and (ii) do not in general imply (iv). Suggestion: try the statement 'x ≤ 1' and exhibit that (i) and (ii) hold but (iv) fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit P(x) and verify conditions; explain vacuous truth aspects if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: (i) and (iii) do not imply (iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that (i) and (iii) (without (ii)) do not in general imply (iv) by constructing a statement P for which (i) and (iii) hold but (iv) fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit P(x) violating fullness but satisfying (iii)'s local-extension condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction-like: (i),(ii),(iii) imply (iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that conditions (i), (ii) and (iii) together imply (iv). Suggestion: if the set of nonnegative x for which P(x) is false is nonempty, look at its greatest lower bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use completeness/GLB argument to rule out a minimal counterexample via (ii) or (iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended real arithmetic true/false
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the following in the extended reals are true or false: (a) (+∞)·0 = 1. (b) (−1/2)·(−∞) = +∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extended arithmetic with usual conventions; justify each T/F answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map non-Archimedean ordered field onto extended reals
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose F is an ordered field properly containing R. (a) Assuming 1.4:4, show F can be mapped onto the extended real number system by a map f that carries each α ∈ R to itself and 'respects' addition and multiplication, i.e., f(α+β)=f(α)+f(β) and f(αβ)=f(α)f(β) except in cases where these operations are not defined in the extended reals. Briefly discuss behavior in the latter cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe images of 'infinite' elements and how arithmetic interacts with ±∞; use order-comparison to classify elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-behavior of map to extended reals
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the map f constructed above behave with respect to the order relation '<'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that f preserves order where defined, and explain comparability and mapping of 'infinitely large' or 'infinitesimal' elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex field true/false
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide true/false for: (a) C is a field under usual operations. (b) For every complex z, Im(conj(z)) = Im(−z). (c) For all complex w,z, Re(wz) = Re(w)Re(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use properties of complex arithmetic and conjugation to evaluate each statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean spaces true/false
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide true/false for statements about Euclidean spaces and norms (see 1.7:0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use basic vector and norm properties, refer to Theorem 1.37(e) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations between |x|, |y|, |x+y| (triangle-type inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for any points x and y of R^k one has |x + y| ≥ |x| − |y| and |x + y| ≥ |y| − |x|. Combine these with Theorem 1.37(e) to analyze possible values of |x + y| when |x| = 1 and |y| = 4, and show existence/nonexistence of pairs achieving allowed values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vector triangle inequality and geometry to construct examples when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nicer proof of Schwarz inequality (real vectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an alternative, more attractive proof of the Schwarz inequality for real vectors using: take a = (a1,...,ak), b = (b1,...,bk); consider the vector a|b| − |a| b and its nonnegativity of dot product with itself; expand and manipulate to reach Schwarz inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address special cases a=0 or b=0 separately; show cancellation of common factor and handle absolute value insertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend Schwarz inequality to complex vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt the previous derivation to complex k-tuples by defining a·b = Σ ai conj(bi) (so a·a real positive for nonzero a), note changes in linearity and commutativity, and use a unimodular scalar γ with |γ|=1 such that γ z = |z| for z=a·b to finish the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain needed conjugation properties and choose γ to convert Re(a·b) to |a·b| when substituting γa for a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz inequality via quadratic formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the real Schwarz inequality by regarding t ↦ (a + t b)·(a + t b) as a real quadratic at^2 + bt + c and using nonnegativity to deduce discriminant ≤ 0, then relate discriminant to Schwarz inequality. For completeness, prove the required discriminant property from scratch (i.e., if discriminant > 0 and a ≠ 0 the quadratic changes sign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to assume previously unproven algebraic facts; handle a = 0 separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedekind cuts true/false
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide true/false for statements about cuts α, β in Q and r*, s* in the cut-construction of R: (a) α + β = {r + s : r ∈ α, s ∈ β}, (b) αβ = {rs : r ∈ α, s ∈ β}, (c) −α = {−r : r ∈ α}, (d) α < β ⇔ α is a proper subset of β, (e) r* = {s : s ≤ r}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions of cut addition/multiplication/negation and ordering in Dedekind-cut construction; justify each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive law details for real numbers via cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the assertion in Step 7 of the proof of Theorem 1.19 that multiplication of cuts satisfies the distributive law by checking a typical list of cases such as (i) α < 0*, β > 0*, γ > 0*, (ii) α < 0*, β > 0*, β + γ < 0*, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through the enumerated sign-cases for α, β, γ and use definitions from Rudin's construction of R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative proof of distributive law (D vs D')
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that axioms (D) and (D') (alternative formulations of distributivity) are equivalent for a set F satisfying addition and multiplication axioms; then use this to reduce checking distributivity for all real numbers to verifying a condition for α ≥ 0* and extend by sign identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow parts (a)-(d): prove each implication, use identities α(−β)=−(αβ), and handle the various sign arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second round of cuts leaves R unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that performing the cut-construction starting from F = R yields a set F' isomorphic to R; more precisely, the map r ↦ r* is an isomorphism (one-to-one and onto, respecting operations and ordering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Rudin's Step 8 assertions and point out the single nontrivial statement to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cuts fail on nonarchimedean fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose F is an ordered field lacking the Archimedean property and carry out the Dedekind-cut construction to get F'. Show that F' fails to satisfy additive inverses axiom (A5); i.e., cuts don't work well on nonarchimedean fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify where Archimedean property was used in Rudin's proof and produce explicit failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove r*s* = (rs)* (cuts multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive rationals r,s prove r*s* = (rs)* by verifying equality of nonpositive elements and describing positive elements; provide inclusions r*s* ⊆ (rs)* and (rs)* ⊆ r*s*, with a construction using rationals t1,t2 and reductions; deduce remaining sign cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow parts (a)-(c) and the hint: choose t1 with 1 < t1 < rs/p and set r' = r/t1, s' = s/t2 as in Rudin's analog; then handle r<0,s>0 case in part (d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite/countable/uncountable true/false (chapter 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide true/false for a list of set-theory statements (2.1:0) including: (a) if f:X→Y and E⊆Y contains exactly one element then f^{-1}(E) contains exactly one element; (b) union of family of subsets ∪_{α∈A} Gα is subset of Y; (c) every proper subset of J is finite; (d) range of any sequence is at most countable; (e) set of rationals r with r^2<2 is countable; (f) every infinite subset of an uncountable set is uncountable; (g) every countable set is a subset of the integers; (h) every subset of integers is at most countable; (i) every finite set is countable; (j)-(m) further statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide T/F and give proofs or counterexamples using elementary set theory and enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite image of countable set is countable
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose E is countable and f:E→Y has infinite image f(E). Show f(E) is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic proof of Theorem 2.8: enumerate E and choose increasing indices n_k giving distinct outputs to form a sequence enumerating f(E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions and cardinalities (A,B,f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A and B and f: A → B examine cases of finiteness/countability/uncountability: (a) for A,B infinite and f one-to-one determine which combinations of countable/uncountable can occur with examples and a proof one cannot occur; (b) extend to finite/countable/uncountable 3×3 chart; (c) similar analysis when f is onto; (d) 3×3 chart analogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide constructive examples for possible cases and logical arguments (implications) ruling out impossible cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality of function sets from countable A
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is countable and B has at least two elements. Show there are uncountably many functions A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with A = J and B = {0,1}; relate to binary sequences and Cantor diagonal / known results about power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric-spaces true/false list
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide true/false for numerous metric-space claims (2.2:0) such as: every unbounded subset of R is infinite; every infinite subset of R is unbounded; interior points belong to the set; subsets of bounded sets bounded; Q dense in R; complements of open sets are closed; unions/intersections properties; convexity claims in R^k, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metric definitions, examples and counterexamples (e.g., bounded infinite sets in R) to justify answers; refer to Rudin where indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible distances among 3 points
rubrics_metrics.description: For any points p,q,r of a metric space show d(p,r) ≥ d(p,q) − d(q,r) and d(p,r) ≥ d(q,r) − d(p,q). Combine with triangle inequality to determine possible values of d(p,r) when given particular d(p,q) and d(q,r), and for each allowed value produce a metric space realizing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply triangle inequality in two forms and construct examples (e.g., on the real line) for realizable values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of open sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a subset E of a metric space X is open iff it is the union of a set of neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definition: open points have a neighborhood contained in E; then union of those neighborhoods equals E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure characterization via ε-neighborhoods
rubrics_metrics.description: Show E̅ = {x ∈ X | (∀ ε > 0) (∃ y ∈ E) d(y,x) < ε}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer this to Rudin's splitting into points of E and limit points; give direct proof from definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of limit points via open sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Show p is a limit point of E iff every open subset G ⊆ X containing p contains some point of E other than p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is equivalent to the neighborhood-based definition; give clear equivalence proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative openness/closedness in subspaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E be open (resp. closed) in X and F ⊆ E. (a) Show F is open relative to E iff F is open in X. (b) Show F is closed relative to E iff F is closed in X. (c)-(d) Give examples where relatively closed subsets of open sets need not be open/closed in X and vice-versa for relatively open subsets of closed sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide proofs for (a) and (b) and explicit counterexamples for (c) and (d) with concrete metric spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary of a subset (∂E) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ∂E as points whose every neighborhood intersects both E and E^c. (a) Show E̅ = E ∪ ∂E. (b) Deduce E closed iff ∂E ⊆ E. (c) E open iff ∂E ⊆ E^c. (d) E both open and closed iff ∂E = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions and set relations between closure, interior and boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent formulations of boundedness
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonempty E ⊆ metric space X show the following equivalent: (a) E bounded. (b) For every q ∈ X ∃ M such that ∀ p ∈ E, d(p,q) < M. (c) ∃ q ∈ E and M such that ∀ p ∈ E, d(p,q) < M. (d) ∃ M such that ∀ p,q ∈ E, d(p,q) < M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove equivalences, noting M values may differ; recall definition of boundedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure as intersection of closed supersets
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the closure E̅ of a subset E is the intersection of all closed subsets of X containing E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard characterization; show E̅ is closed and contains E and is minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of bounded set is bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if E is bounded then its closure E̅ is also bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distance bound from some center and pass limit to closure points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding bounded perfect subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a metric space. (a) If E is perfect and A is open, show E ∩ A is perfect. (b) Deduce that if X has a nonempty perfect subset then it has a bounded nonempty perfect subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local compactness of open sets intersecting perfect sets and choice of appropriate open balls to obtain bounded perfect subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifying a metric to get another metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Given metric d on X: (a) show d'(x,y)=d(x,y)^{1/2} is a metric and induces the same open sets as d. (b) Is d''(x,y)=d(x,y)^2 also having same open sets? (c) For which f:[0,∞)→[0,∞) is df(x,y)=f(d(x,y)) a metric for every metric d?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check metric axioms; for (c) characterize monotonicity/subadditivity/concavity conditions needed (e.g., subadditive concave functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-closed set has no largest closed subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E ⊆ X not closed. (a) Show there is no largest closed subset contained in E: any closed F ⊆ E can be enlarged by adding one more limit point still within E. (b) Show there is always a largest open subset of X contained in E but in general no smallest open subset containing E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closure and limit-point arguments and refer to Exercise 2:R9 for part (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of two definitions of 'dense' in R
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for E ⊆ R the definition (i) between any x<y ∃ p∈E with x<p<y is equivalent to (ii) every point of R is a limit point of E or point of E (the metric-space definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove each implication using completeness of order topology on R and neighborhoods/intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: n-adic metric on Z
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix integer n>1. For nonzero integer s let e_n(s) be largest a with s divisible by n^a (0 if s=0). Define d_n(s,t)=n^{-e_n(s−t)} (and 0 if s=t). Show this is a metric and satisfies the ultrametric inequality d_n(p,q) ≤ max(d_n(p,r),d_n(r,q)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show strong triangle inequality using divisibility properties; note when n is prime this gives the p-adic metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated limit sets L^n
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for every positive integer n there exists a subset E of some metric space X such that L^{n−1}(E) ≠ ∅ but L^n(E) = ∅ (where L denotes the set of limit points and L^0(E)=E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct appropriate nested sequences or use subsets of R to obtain prescribed finite iteration of limit-set nonemptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit points in terms of closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Show p is a limit point of E iff p ∈ E̅ − {p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate definition of limit point to closure and set difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed balls Vr(p) identity and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: For p∈X and r>0 let Vr(p) be closure of Nr(p). (a) Show Vr(p) = {q ∈ X | d(p,q) ≤ r} (i.e., Vr(p) is closed). (b) Give four examples (X,p,r) exhibiting all combinations of equalities/inequalities among Nr(p), Nr(p) (closure?), and Vr(p): all three equal; equality at first ⊆ not at second; equality at second not first; all distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct metric spaces (discrete, usual R with particular radii, etc.) to realize each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite metric space may not embed in R^k
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a 4-point metric space X = {w,x,y,z} with distances: d(w,others)=1, distances among the other three = 2. (a) Verify metric axioms. (b) Show no distance-preserving embedding of X into R^k exists. (c) Note that every 3-point subset can embed, and ask for a 5-point analog where every 4-point subset embeds but whole 5-point set does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric constraints in Euclidean space (e.g., isosceles triangles and distances) to show impossibility and suggest combinatorial constructions for larger examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite metric space has uncountably many open sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be infinite. (a) Show X has a countable family of pairwise disjoint neighborhoods {N_{r_i}(p_i)} (i∈J). (b) Deduce X has uncountably many open sets (e.g., unions of those neighborhoods for sequences (s_i) of 0's and 1's).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct disjoint neighborhoods inductively using infinite subsets and use binary sequences to get 2^{ℵ0} distinct open sets; note special cases like {1/n}∪{0} require avoiding 0 as a chosen center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated interior and closure operations identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how many different sets can result from successive application of closure and interior operators to a set E. (a) Show (E^∘)^∘ = E^∘ and (E̅)̅ = E̅ so repeated same operator stabilizes. (b) Show (E^∘)̅^∘ = E^∘ (and other identity) and deduce limitations on number of distinct sets obtainable by alternating closure and interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard Kuratowski-style closure/interior identities (Kuratowski 14-set theorem context) and hints referencing Rudin's exercises.
